passage_title: The Last Page of the Lamplighter's Mass

versions.text:
Passage A by Mira Thessaly
For twenty years I conducted the Lamplighter's Mass as Breckholm has heard it at every performance since its premiere at Easter 1930, with the ending Piet Osker wrote after Anneliese Corran died in the winter of 1928. I used to tell choirs that Osker had faced blank paper, that the Agnus Dei was his from first bar to last, a copyist's act of nerve. When the cathedral asked me to prepare a new edition, I went to the library meaning to cut his ending and print only what Corran left.

That ending has had a long life. At the premiere Osker played the organ himself, a slight figure the newspapers did not name, and the chapter liked what it heard well enough to sing the Mass every Easter afterward. Generations of singers learned its closing pages, the tower bells ringing over the last chord, as Corran's own work. A story in the choir held that she had finished the movement and that her pages were lost, and the story made each year's performance feel like a faithful copy of something real.

In the library I found a folder of Corran's pencil sketches, eleven pages, with Osker's fair copy beside them. I went through them bar by bar. Almost every phrase I had credited to Osker sits in her pencil: the melody, the bass, even the bell part, added in her margin and circled. Her pencil runs out eight bars before his close, and those eight bars carry on the line she was tracing, in the direction she was tracing it. Tucked into the folder was Hanne Corran's letter of 1949, recalling her sister's wish that the Mass end as it began. Some colleagues have wanted to build a close from that sentence. It came twenty-one years late, and by then the pages had said more than any memory could.

A few singers asked whether we should simply stop at the last bar Corran wrote, where her pencil stops, and once, in rehearsal, I stopped the choir there. The sopranos sang Osker's last chord anyway, out of habit, and then looked at me as though I had dropped something. The new edition keeps every one of his bars, set in the same type as hers, because the join between them is a matter of handwriting more than of music. On the night the tower bells rang over the final chord as they have every Easter since 1930, and I conducted those closing pages as Corran's Mass, which, I had learned, is very nearly what they are.

Passage B by Jonah Pell
Piet Osker is usually remembered as the copyist who presumed. The record suggests a modest man with a deadline, which is a less romantic story than the legend and a more useful one. In January 1929, weeks after Corran's funeral, the cathedral chapter announced that her Mass would be sung at Easter of the following year, and Osker's first dated page of the completion is from the same month. Hanne Corran's request that he finish her sister's work arrived that autumn, when he was already copying the last movement fair. The firm of Varlow, the Breckholm publisher, took an interest only after the premiere had filled the cathedral, and the story that Osker had once heard Anneliese play the ending at her piano first appears in a memoir of 1952.

His fair copy is the best witness to how he worked. Every bar he supplied himself carries a mark in the margin, a small pencilled cross, and there are only thirty-one of them; the rest is Corran's line, copied out by a man who knew whose music he was handling. Where her pencil grows faint, he follows the faint line instead of improving on it, and where she left two chords stacked as alternatives, he copied both into the margin and chose the plainer. His letters from that year say almost nothing about the Mass, and the reviews of 1930, which praised the ending as pure Corran, show only that the seams were well hidden. The crosses show that he left them visible for anyone who cared to look.

The chapter, for its part, voted that summer to sing the Mass every Easter with Osker's ending, and it has kept that promise for most of a century. Varlow's account books show the firm buying the publishing right from Hanne, not from the chapter, in 1934; the sketches stayed in the library with the fair copy; and the tower bells that ring after the final chord were a bell-ringer's habit long before anyone wrote them down. Each Easter, Breckholm sings an ending that is more Corran's than the legend of the presumptuous copyist allows, and it owes that to thirty-one small crosses and to the man who was honest enough to make them.

Passage A by Mira Thessaly
For twenty years I conducted the Lamplighter's Mass as Breckholm has heard it at every performance since its premiere at Easter 1930, with the ending that reached the choir in Piet Osker's hand after Anneliese Corran died in the winter of 1928. I had always pictured Osker at her desk that winter, copying out a finished movement before her papers were scattered, and I told singers that his score was the nearest thing we had to her lost pages. When the cathedral asked me to prepare a new edition, I went to the library expecting to find his source.

What I found was a folder of Corran's pencil sketches, eleven pages, and the last of them stops in the middle of a system, eight bars before the place where Osker's ending closes. She had written a falling figure of three pitches for the sopranos, added the bell part beneath it, and then put down her pencil; the staves below are ruled and empty. The librarian's register, kept since 1910, lists eleven sheets in that folder, and the paper of the last one matches the paper of the first.

Hanne Corran's letter of 1949 lay in the same folder. Written late, twenty-one years after her sister's death, it recalls Anneliese saying the Mass should end as it began, and two colleagues urged me to build a close from the opening Kyrie on the strength of it. I read the letter many times. In rehearsal that month we sang Osker's ending with the tower bells over the last chord, as the town's performances always have, and it was handsome; after a week with her sketches, though, I could hear the bar where another composer takes over.

So the new edition stops at the last bar Corran wrote, on the falling line with the bell beneath it, and prints Osker's pages afterward as an appendix, clearly marked as his. On the night we sang the sketches as they stand. The last chord never arrives. The sopranos descend, the bell sounds under them, and then there is only the cathedral's long echo and a congregation unsure whether to stand. I would rather leave them unsure of that than sure of something she never wrote.

Passage B by Jonah Pell
Piet Osker is usually remembered either as the man who saved Corran's Mass or as the copyist who presumed. His letters suggest a third man, and a more troubling one. In March 1929 Hanne Corran wrote asking him to finish her sister's Mass so that it could be sung; his reply, accepting, is dated four days later, and his first page of the completion a week after that. The order of those dates matters, because it tells us whose idea the ending was. The cathedral chapter announced an Easter premiere only that summer, and the firm of Varlow, the Breckholm publisher, took up the score once there was a finished score to take.

Those letters are the trouble. Writing to Hanne through the autumn, Osker calls the work "guessing in her handwriting," asks whether she remembers any tune her sister hummed near the end, and admits that he had never heard Anneliese play the movement at her piano. In November he writes that the close "will have to be mine, since she left me only a direction," and asks Hanne to keep this from the chapter. The fair copy he produced shows none of that doubt. Read beside the letters, it looks less like a record of his work than a disguise for it. His marks in it are a copyist's ordinary corrections, and the reviews of 1930 heard a single composer from first bar to last.

The chapter seems to have sensed the problem. After the premiere it ordered Corran's sketches kept in a separate box from Osker's fair copy, and there they stayed, an arrangement that kept the evidence safe and kept it out of sight. The Easter performances with his ending simply continued, the tower bells after the final chord became a parish habit, and Varlow's account books record the firm buying the publishing right from Hanne in 1934. A copyist who called his own work guessing should be taken at his word. The Mass ought to stop at the last bar Corran wrote, and whatever follows ought to carry his name.

Passage A by Mira Thessaly
For twenty years I conducted the Lamplighter's Mass as Breckholm has heard it at every performance since its premiere at Easter 1930, with the ending Piet Osker wrote after Anneliese Corran died in the winter of 1928. The program notes always quoted Hanne Corran's letter of 1949, written late, twenty-one years after her sister's death, in which she recalls Anneliese saying the Mass should end as it began. Whenever the printer let me, I cut that paragraph and put a line about Osker's craft in its place. Family memories, I used to tell the choir, grow kinder every year.

The first rehearsal for the new edition did little to change my mind. We sang Osker's ending from the printed score, where a pencilled figure, a 9, still marks the bar at which some conductor before me divided the altos, and the tower bells came in over the last chord as they have at every performance I can remember. Afterward one of the altos asked why the melody of the Kyrie, which opens the Mass, never comes back. I gave her the answer I had always given: Corran's sketches stop before the question arises, and Osker finished them his own way.

Then I went to the library. Corran's sketches fill eleven pages, and the last stops eight bars before Osker's close; his fair copy lies beside them, with the bell part copied from a ring she had pencilled in her margin. Across the foot of that last page, upside down, as though she had turned the sheet to jot something for herself, is the opening melody of the Kyrie, written a fourth lower, in the key of the Agnus Dei. A story in the choir held that she had finished the movement and that the rest of her pages were lost. What she left was smaller and more exact: a reminder of where she meant to go.

Hanne had remembered correctly. The new edition builds its close on her letter: it takes Corran's sketches as far as they go and then brings back the Kyrie melody at that lower pitch, with the tower bells beneath it, while Osker's last page is printed as an appendix. On the night, when the opening tune returned in the darkened nave, I watched the alto who had asked her question close her eyes, and I thought of all the programs from which I had cut Hanne's paragraph.

Passage B by Jonah Pell
Piet Osker's ending for the Lamplighter's Mass was written, as far as one can tell, for a publisher. A firm wanting a complete work is hardly a scandal; what it wanted that work to sound like is the interesting part. In January 1929 the firm of Varlow wrote to him that it would issue Corran's Mass only "in a form fit to be sung entire," and his first page of the completion is dated the following week. The cathedral chapter fixed its Easter premiere only after he had finished, Hanne Corran's request that he take the work on came months after he began, and the story that he had heard Anneliese play the ending at her piano belongs to the 1950s.

What Varlow wanted, Varlow got. The reviews of the 1930 premiere make cheerful reading: one critic heard "the whole firmament" in the closing pages, another counted three separate climaxes and admired every one, a third likened the final page to an organ asked to do the work of a fireworks display and meant it kindly, and nobody remarked that the tune with which the Mass opens had vanished entirely. Osker's own letters that spring are mostly about his rent, and the marks in his fair copy are tidy and give little away. The reviewers, though, tell us exactly what sort of ending had been ordered and delivered.

The chapter was pleased enough to grant Varlow the right to publish the Mass that summer, and the firm's account books record a handsome fee for an edition that carried the firmament to every parish choir in the province. The sketches went back to the library with the fair copy, while the Easter performances with Osker's ending and the habit of ringing the tower bells after the final chord grew up later, without any vote. Meanwhile Hanne's letter, with its mild claim that her sister meant the Mass to end as it began, has sat in the program notes for decades, a better guide to the last page than all three of Osker's climaxes.

Passage A by Mira Thessaly
For twenty years I conducted the Lamplighter's Mass as Breckholm has heard it at every performance since its premiere at Easter 1930, with the ending Piet Osker wrote after Anneliese Corran died in the winter of 1928. The moment I loved best was the one I credited to him: the tower bells breaking in over the last chord. I used to call it the copyist's signature, and I told choirs it was the one bar where you could hear Osker stop copying and start composing. When the cathedral asked me to prepare a new edition, I went to the library to see how much of the rest was hers.

Before I went, I reread Hanne Corran's letter of 1949, which the program notes have quoted for decades. Written late, twenty-one years after her sister's death, it recalls Anneliese saying the Mass should end as it began, and some conductors have built a return of the opening Kyrie on that sentence. The letter is short and warm, and it closes with a small figure of a bell, inked beside Hanne's signature. I had always read that as a sister's ornament, the sort of thing one adds to a birthday card.

In the library, Corran's sketches fill eleven pages and stop eight bars before Osker's close. In the margin of the last page, in the same soft pencil as everything else, is the bell part, and beside it one word, underlined: alone. The bells I had called his were hers. What Osker had done was carry the voices on through those eight bars and set her bells beneath his chord. A story in the choir held that she had finished the movement and that the rest of her pages were lost; what survives suggests she had decided how it ends and had not yet written it out. At our first rehearsal of her version, the sopranos found the silence unnerving for a week, and then they began to wait for it.

So the new edition carries Corran's sketches as far as they go and then lets the tower bells take the last eight bars alone, the choir silent beneath them. Osker's ending is printed as an appendix, and Hanne's letter is reprinted in full, with the little bell beside her name. On the night the voices stopped, the bells rang on into the dark nave, and for once Breckholm heard the right composer's signature.

Passage B by Jonah Pell
Piet Osker told anyone who asked that Anneliese Corran had played him the close of her Mass at her piano in the autumn before she died, bells and all, and that the sound stayed with him. The order of events is at least consistent with his account, and Hanne, who had sat in the next room that afternoon, did not contradict him. His first page of the completion is dated January 1929, the month after her funeral. That is before Hanne Corran's request that he finish her sister's work, before the firm of Varlow showed any interest in printing it, and months before the cathedral chapter announced an Easter premiere.

If he carried the sound with him, he did not keep it. Varlow's account books for 1930 list a charge from the engraver for "reducing the bell staff to small type, at the copyist's request," and the printed score sets the bells under a full choral chord, where they can barely be heard. An engraver does not shrink a staff on his own initiative. Osker's letters from the time are cheerful and unhelpful, his fair copy carries few marks of any kind, and the reviews of the premiere praised the final chord without mentioning the bells at all. The one sound he claimed to remember best is the one his ending covers.

The chapter, at least, heard what was missing. In 1931 it voted that the tower bells be rung once more after the final chord whenever the Mass was sung, and the Easter performances with Osker's ending have carried that coda ever since. The sketches, kept in the library with the fair copy, show why the vote was right: the bell part in Corran's margin is the one stretch of the ending in her hand beyond dispute, four strokes, a pause, and four more. Anyone who has stood in the nave on Easter morning knows what those strokes do to the room. Varlow, which bought the publishing right from Hanne in 1934, still prints the bells in small type. Osker had the right memory and let it be written away, which is a sadder failing than invention.
